newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Auditors appointed to hunt Swiss Holocaust money.
newsitem.headline: Auditors appointed to hunt Swiss Holocaust money.

text.p: The independent panel probing allegations that Swiss banks are sitting on unclaimed wealth of Holocaust victims has selected three leading auditing firms to hunt for any missing assets, it said on Tuesday.
The committee, formed in May by Jewish groups and Swiss bankers, said the search of banks' old records and questioning of potential witnesses could take until mid-1998.

The Independent Committee of Eminent Persons, headed by former U.S. central bank chief Paul Volcker, said in a statement it had picked accounting firms Arthur Andersen, KPMG Peat Marwick and Price Waterhouse to conduct the politically sensitive search.

The search was triggered by persistent accusations from outraged Jewish groups and a U.S. Senator Alfonse D'Amato that Swiss banks profited cynically from the Holocaust and then stonewalled relatives trying to find family members' wealth.
Swiss banks deny the charges, but agreed to the probe.

The Swiss Bankers Association (SBA) said early this year that banks had discovered 38.7 million Swiss francs ($30.5 million) in accounts opened by customers before the end of World War Two and dormant since at least 1985.

Since then, "some banks have identified additional accounts and amounts of foreign customers which the SBA estimates could increase the total amount of such dormant accounts by 10 percent," the panel said.

Not all these funds were necessarily owned by Jews killed in the Holocaust, Swiss bankers say, adding the Swiss government had ordered banks in 1962 to conduct a similar sweep for dormant accounts of Nazi victims.
That turned up 9.5 million francs (now worth $7.5 million), of which 75 percent was returned to heirs and the rest given to Switzerland's Jewish community and a group that helps refugees.
